extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply Coleridge's critical criteria for writing and judging poetry and poetic prose — focusing on diction, logic, imagination, metre, and common faults of young writers. Useful for literary students and poets working on style and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity, turgid diction, and new-coined double epithets (faults)
rubrics_metrics.description: The early critics objected to 'obscurity, a general turgiduesa of diction, and a profusion of new-coined double epithets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anti-patterns to be avoided; Coleridge states he pruned 'double epithets' and sought to 'tame the swell and glitter both of thought and diction.' If these faults exist, simplify and remove ornament that obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for manly simplicity / natural diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Austerer and more natural style is superior: Coleridge praises the 'manly simplicity of the Grecian' and the 'natural diction' exemplified by Bowles and Cowper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for plainness and naturalness in expression; favor diction that conveys thought directly rather than dressing prose-thoughts in poetic finery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic of poetry: reason for every word and its position
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge: 'poetry...has a logic of its own...in the truly great poets, there is a reason assignable, not only for every word, but for the position of every word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words (and their order) with care; each word's presence and placement should be defensible by its contribution to sense, feeling, or poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return-value: enduring re-readability as a test of essential poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's aphorism: 'not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return, with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power and claims the name of essential poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by whether readers will repeatedly return to it with pleasure; transitory cleverness that doesn't invite re-reading is inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-translatability criterion (vicious diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge: 'whatever lines can be translated into other words of the same language without diminution of their significance ... are so far vicious in their diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrasing that is paraphrase-able without loss of effect; prefer diction and phrasing whose particular words/arrangement are essential to the poem's meaning or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine natural thought with natural diction; reconcile heart and head
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge praises poets who 'combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the first who reconciled the heart with the head.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for unity between feeling and intellect: thoughts should be expressed in diction that fits their emotional truth rather than intellectual ornament alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hackneyed similes, stock phrases, and clichéd imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge recounts his master's interdiction of words and phrases (e.g., 'lyre', 'harp', 'Pegasus') and repeating similes (Alexander and Clytus) as overused and unapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban common introductions/transitions and worn metaphors; seek apt, fresh images rather than ready-made classical allusions that fit every subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three young-writer sins: doleful egotism, false simplicity, indiscriminate elaborate language
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's satirical sonnets target (1) 'the spirit of doleful egotism, and the recurrence of favourite phrases', (2) 'low, creeping language and thoughts, under the pretence of simplicity', and (3) 'the indiscriminate use of elaborate...language and imagery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young writers should avoid self-pitying egotism and stock phrases, beware affected 'simplicity' that is merely weak expression, and refrain from indiscriminate ornament and extravagant imagery used without necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's worthy feelings vs. mere novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge excludes 'the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader, and the desire of exciting wonderment at his powers in the author' from 'worthy feelings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value feelings and effects that are genuinely moving or meaningful rather than novelty for its own sake or trickiness intended merely to astonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and metrical diction impose conditions on choice of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge notes 'language of metrical composition...why and wherein essentially different from that of prose — origin and elements of metre — its necessary consequences and the conditions thereby imposed on the metrical writer in the choice of his diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing verse, select diction that suits metrical demands; metre shapes allowable word order, sound, and economy — don't force prose phrasing into strict metre without regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between neutral style and truly poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: He discusses 'the neutral style, or that common to prose and poetry' and examines the 'true nature of poetic diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of styles that sit between prose and poetry; determine when heightened diction is necessary, and when the neutral style better serves clarity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sacrificing passion to intellect or ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge contrasts elder poets who 'sacrificed the passion...to the subtleties of intellect' with moderns who sacrifice 'both heart and head to point and drapery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize intellectual cleverness or decorative ornament at the expense of sincere feeling and coherent thought; balance is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination (esemplastic power) as central poetic faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge signals chapters 'On the imagination or esemplastic power' and treats imagination's nature and genesis as central to poetic creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the imagination's synthesizing role when evaluating or producing poetry: creativity is not mere association but an organizing power that shapes feeling and image into unified forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical and classical exemplars to justify diction and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout, Coleridge appeals to Homer, Theocritus, Chaucer, Milton, Shakespeare, and Greek poets to defend natural diction and metrical practice (e.g., arguing against couplet-closure habit of moderns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputing style choices, ground arguments in examples from canonical works; compare meter, diction, and function across traditions to justify choices rather than relying only on fashion.
